'''Athīr al-Dīn al-Mufaḍḍal ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Mufaḍḍal al-Samarqandī al-Abharī''' ([[Persian language|Persian]]):  اثیرالدین مُفَضَّل بن عمر بن مَفَضَّل سمرقندی ابهری; d. 1262 or 1265<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Citation |last=Terrier |first=Mathieu |title='Allama al-Ḥillī |date=2020 |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Medieval Philosophy: Philosophy between 500 and 1500 |pages=129–139 |editor-last=Lagerlund |editor-first=Henrik |url=https://link.springer.com/referenceworkentry/10.1007/978-94-024-1665-7_584 |access-date=2024-09-23 |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-94-024-1665-7_584 |isbn=978-94-024-1665-7|url-access=subscription }}</ref> also known as '''Athīr al-Dīn al-Munajjim''' (اثیرالدین منجم) was an Iranian Muslim [[polymath]], [[Early Islamic philosophy|philosopher]], [[Islamic astronomer|astronomer]], [[Islamic astrologer|astrologer]] and [[Islamic mathematician|mathematician]]. Other than his influential writings, he had many disciples.{{fact|date=December 2024}}

==Life==
His birthplace is contested among sources. According to the ''[[Encyclopaedia of Islam]]''<ref name=":0">{{cite journal|last1=Heidrun|first1=Eichner|title=Al-Abharī, Athīr al-Dīn|journal=Encyclopaedia of Islam, Three|date=December 2008|url=https://referenceworks.brillonline.com/entries/encyclopaedia-of-islam-3/al-abhari-athir-al-din-COM_26284?s.num=204&s.rows=100&s.start=200|publisher=Brill|access-date=20 February 2017|language=en}}</ref> and the ''[[Encyclopaedia Islamica]]'',<ref name="islamica">{{cite web |title=Athir al-Din al-Abhari |url=https://www.cgie.org.ir/fa/publication/entryview/3937 |access-date=5 February 2017 |website=Encyclopedia Islamica |publisher=[[CGIE]]}}</ref> he was born in [[Abhar]], a small town between [[Qazvin]] and [[Zanjan, Iran|Zanjan]] in the North-West of Iran. The claim of G.C. Anawati making him a native of Mosul in Iraq, taken from the fact that al-Abharī was educated by a scientist from Mosul, [[Kamāl al-Dīn ibn Yūnus|Kamāl al-Dīn ibn Yūnus al-Mawṣilī]], must also been dismissed.<ref name=":1" /> None of his oldest biographers mentioned Mosul as his birthplace,<ref name="islamica" /> and al-Abharī himself indicated that he had gone to Mosul for this purpose.<ref name=":1" /> Beside the city of Abhar, the epithet al-Abharī could suggest that he or his ancestors originally stem from the Abhar tribe.{{sfn|Sarıoğlu|2007}} 

In his youth al-Abharī was a student of the theologian [[Fakhr al-Din al-Razi|Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī]], probably in the city of [[Ghazni]] or [[Herat]]. Beside philosophy and logic, from al-Rāzī it is likely that al-Abharī received an orthodox Sunni instruction in theology (kalām), jurisprudence (fiqh), and Qur’anic exegesis (tafsīr).<ref name=":1" /> When Mongol took [[Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire|Khwarezmian Empire]], al-Abharī, in 1228 he flew to [[Erbil]], then to [[Damascus]], where he studied to Muḥyī al-Dīn Muḥammad b. Sa‘īd b. Nadī.<ref name=":1" /> Then he went to Mosul, where he studied mathematics, especially astronomy, under the direction of Kamāl al-Dīn al-Mawṣilī.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

Among his students were [[Najm al-Din al-Qazwini al-Katibi]], [[Zakariya al-Qazwini|Abū Zakariya al-Qazwini]], and [[Ibn Khallikan|Ibn Khallikān]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/ocm65764986 |title=The biographical encyclopedia of astronomers |date=2007 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-0-387-31022-0 |editor-last=Hockey |editor-first=Thomas A. |series=Springer reference |location=New York |oclc=ocm65764986 |editor-last2=Trimble |editor-first2=Virginia |editor-last3=Bracher |editor-first3=Katherine}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

According to most accounts, al-Abharī died in Mosul between 660/1261–62 and 663/1264–65,<ref name=":0" /> during the reign of [[Hulegu Khan|Khān Hülegü]].<ref name=":1" />

==Works==
; Astronomy
* Risāla fī al-hayʾa (رساله الهیئة; lit. Treatise on astronomy).
* Mukhtaṣar fī al-hayʾa (مختصر فی علم الهیئة; lit. Epitome on astronomy).
* Kashf al-ḥaqāʾiq fī taḥrīr al-daqāʾiq (كشف الحقائق فی تحریر الدقائق), where he accepts the view that the [[celestial bodies]] do not change and maintains that stars have volition and it is the source of their motion.{{sfn|Sarıoğlu|2007}}

; Mathematics
* Several works on Iṣlāḥ (اصلاح; lit. Correction) of [[Euclid]], one of which is an attempt to prove the [[parallel postulate]], which was commented upon and criticized by [[Shams al-Dīn al-Samarqandī]].{{sfn|Sarıoğlu|2007}}

; Philosophy
* {{transliteration|ar|ALA|Hidāyah al-Hikmah}} (هدایةالحکمه; lit. Guide on Philosophy): a book dealing with the complete cycle of Hikmat, i.e., [[logic]], [[natural philosophy]], and [[metaphysics]].
* ''{{transliteration|ar|ALA|Isāghūjī fi al-Manṭiq}}'' (ایساغوجی فی المنطق; Commentary on [[Porphyry (philosopher)|Porphyry]]'s ''Isagoge''), a treatise on [[logic]]. Latin Translation by [[Thomas Obicini]]; ''Īsāghūkhī, Isagoge. Id est, breve Introductorium Arabicum in Scientiam Logices: cum versione latina: ac theses Sanctae Fidei. R. P. F. Thomae Novariensis''  (1625).
